prize_parts.citation: For the nonlinear stochastic equation of kinetic roughening and the universality class that bears their names, with Parisi's co-authorship acknowledged in the citation context

statement.case_for: The Kardar-Zhang equation is the minimal nonlinear stochastic model of interface growth, and it defines a universality class that now reaches well beyond growth fronts: exact one-dimensional exponents, Tracy-Widom statistics tied to random-matrix theory, and quantitative confirmation in liquid-crystal turbulence experiments. That is the combination I value most: a simple mechanism, an unexpectedly general result, rigorous exact solutions and contact with experiment. It is nearly four decades old, so there is no maturity concern. Having reread the other seven ballots I still find the physical case clean, but I accept that nobody else ranked it, so I present it as my preferred view and not as a likely consensus.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is attribution. The 1986 paper has three authors and Parisi, who already shares the 2021 prize, is not in the credited names, so a Kardar-Zhang prize would split an original trio and a committee could reasonably hesitate. Spohn's contribution is the later exact-solution programme, which is mathematically deep but is a different achievement from the proposal. Strict experimental realisations of the KPZ class are also fewer than the theory's reach suggests. And no colleague placed this candidate in the top eight, so it may be a niche theoretical preference that does not survive the full committee.

responses.point: Ranks the optical lattice clock first: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's 1e-18 realisation changed what can be measured, with independent confirmation from several laboratories and a clean two-person credit.
responses.response: I agree that this is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and the magic-wavelength idea is exactly the kind of simple mechanism (cancelling the light shift) that I admire. My reservation is the one Eriksson and Pearce touch on: much of the impact is metrological, and the frequency-comb work was honoured in 2005. I do not think that overlap is disqualifying, since the lattice scheme is a distinct idea, but I would want the citation to name the magic-wavelength concept explicitly, so I list B030 as my first alternative and not as a rival I oppose.

responses.point: Argues for the lattice clock as a genuinely new idea resting on atomic polarizability physics, confirmed across Tokyo, Boulder, Paris and elsewhere, and notes that the credit needs no third person.
responses.response: Your point about independent comparisons agreeing at the 1e-18 level is persuasive on maturity and I cannot match it with KPZ, where strict experimental realisations are fewer. Where I differ is on the claim that this strength should settle ranking: broad support in opening ballots is not the same as scientific priority, and a prize recognising a universal statistical mechanism deserves a serious hearing even with a single advocate. I would be content to see B030 win, but not before the committee has tested the attribution argument for B049 on its merits.

responses.point: Ranks topological insulators first because Kane-Mele and the HgTe observation of helical edge transport are original and lasting, noting that Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes, and the 3D work are not in the credited names.
responses.response: We agree on the importance, and I ranked B058 fourth for that reason. Where I am more cautious is the credit: if the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is excluded, the prize may look incomplete, and the 2016 prize already touched topological matter. I would keep Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the workable trio but I want the citation to be specific about the quantum spin Hall effect and not about topology in general, otherwise the overlap objection becomes harder to answer.

responses.point: Ranks the IceCube discovery first as a detector-driven opening of a new observational window, with the diffuse flux confirmed in several channels, while asking for expert review of attribution among Halzen, Karle and Spiering and the AMANDA and Baikal precursors.
responses.response: I share your caution on attribution, and I would add that Kroll rated the same discovery slightly early because source identification is incomplete. The diffuse flux itself is secure, so I do not think the discovery is premature, but a three-person credit among hundreds of collaborators is a harder allocation than the lattice clock or the KPZ pair. I can see the prize being well deserved, yet I cannot judge the instrumentation history, so I leave B020 out of my alternatives and defer to you and Danielsson on it.

responses.point: Ranks the Higgs observation first as the decisive experimental verification of the mechanism of mass, which the 2013 prize recognised only on the theory side, and admits that the choice of three among the credited names is contestable.
responses.response: The scientific importance is not in doubt and I ranked it eighth only because attribution to collaborations of thousands seems arbitrary, and I defer to particle physicists on the ranking. I would press you on whether a three-person subset of spokespeople and detector leaders can be defended as the 'discovery', since you yourself note that Della Negra and Evans have strong claims that cannot be accommodated. If you can show that the choice is robust, I would move it up; at present it seems to me that this is the candidate where the three-person limit does the most damage.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would accept a Kardar-Zhang prize that omits Parisi, who is a co-author of the 1986 paper and already a laureate.
Whether the later exact solutions (Johansson, Prahofer-Spohn, Amir-Corwin-Quastel, Sasamoto-Spohn) and Spohn's role should count as part of the achievement or as a separate contribution.

How the committee weighs a precision-measurement invention (B030) against a conceptual statistical-mechanics result, and whether the 2005 frequency-metrology prize makes the lattice clock look incremental.
Whether the quantum spin Hall prize (B058) can be worded to avoid overlap with the 2016 topology prize and to handle the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from the provided profile; I have no recorded collaboration with Kardar, Zhang, Spohn or any other credited name. I note only that I am in the Gothenburg physics environment alongside Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers), and that Johansson's top-ranked B029 is in a field he is close to; that is institutional proximity, not a conflict for my own preferred configuration.
